subject: Chemistry
central_question: How does the nitrogen lone pair control the structure, basicity, preparation, reactions and diazonium chemistry of amines?
in_scope_units: Structure, pyramidal geometry and classification of amines.
Common and IUPAC nomenclature of aliphatic and aromatic amines.
Preparation by reduction, ammonolysis, nitrile and amide reduction, Gabriel synthesis and Hoffmann bromamide degradation.
Basicity of aliphatic and aromatic amines, including inductive, resonance, solvation and steric effects.
Chemical reactions of amines and tests distinguishing primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
Preparation, physical properties and reactions of arenediazonium salts.
Use of diazonium salts in substitution and azo-coupling synthesis.
banned_topics: Amide chemistry beyond reduction and Hoffmann degradation.
Detailed heterocyclic amines and alkaloid structures beyond the introductory examples.
Full dye technology beyond azo-coupling reactions.

known_pitfalls.claim: Tertiary amines have the highest boiling point because they have three alkyl groups.
known_pitfalls.correction: Among isomeric amines, primary amines usually boil highest because they form the strongest intermolecular hydrogen-bond network; tertiary amines lack N–H bonds.

known_pitfalls.claim: Aniline is more basic than ammonia because phenyl is a carbon group.
known_pitfalls.correction: Aniline is less basic because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring and is less available for protonation.

known_pitfalls.claim: Gabriel synthesis prepares aromatic primary amines efficiently.
known_pitfalls.correction: Aryl halides do not undergo the required nucleophilic substitution, so Gabriel synthesis is used for aliphatic primary amines.

known_pitfalls.claim: Hoffmann bromamide degradation retains the same carbon count.
known_pitfalls.correction: The product primary amine has one carbon less than the starting amide.

known_pitfalls.claim: Arenediazonium salts are prepared and stored at room temperature.
known_pitfalls.correction: They are prepared at 273–278 K because many are unstable and decompose at higher temperatures.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 9.1 on ammonolysis and successive alkylation.
Use NCERT Example 9.2 for nitrile-based chain extension conversions.
Use NCERT Example 9.3 or the adjacent Hoffmann discussion for one-carbon loss.
Apply NCERT Example 9.4 to basic-strength orders.
Finish with NCERT Example 9.5 on diazonium-mediated multistep conversion.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter Exercises are numbered 9.1 to 9.14 and cover nomenclature, preparation, basicity, tests, reactions, diazonium salts and conversions.
